---
title: "Airhouse"
description: "Oxygen's managed warehouse, where your data lands and is queried from"
---

**Airhouse** is Oxygen's managed warehouse, where your data lands and where
the [semantic model](/guide/build/semantic-model/simple-model) and agents
query it. It speaks the Postgres wire protocol, runs queries on
[DuckDB](https://duckdb.org), and stores tables in open formats with
[DuckLake](https://ducklake.select). It has three parts:

- The **data plane** checks every statement against the caller's credentials,
  role, and limits before DuckDB runs it.
- The **control plane** provisions a database for each workspace and mints
  short-lived credentials on demand.
- **Storage** keeps each database's catalog and Parquet files isolated from
  every other database.

<Frame caption="Airhouse checks every statement before DuckDB runs it, hands out only short-lived credentials, and keeps each database's catalog and files isolated in open formats.">

## Why it matters

- **No long-lived keys.** Agents, pipelines, and apps never hold a warehouse
  password. Oxygen mints a credential when one is needed, scoped to the
  caller's role, and it expires on its own.
- **Isolation by default.** Each workspace gets its own database, with its own
  catalog, storage location, users, and query limits.
- **Open formats.** Tables are standard Parquet with a DuckLake catalog, so the
  data stays readable with open tooling and is never locked in.
- **Works with existing tools.** Any Postgres-compatible client or BI tool can
  connect without a new driver.

## Performance

We measured Airhouse with [ClickBench](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickBench),
an open analytics benchmark: 43 queries over a 100-million-row table, run with
ClickBench's own harness on its reference machine, an AWS c6a.4xlarge (16 vCPU,
32 GB). Airhouse ran on that single machine, with its tables as Parquet in S3
and the DuckLake catalog in Postgres on the same machine. This is a benchmark
setup, not the managed service your workspace runs on. All 43 queries
completed, and a warm run of the full suite took 34.3 seconds.

ClickBench scores each system by dividing its time on every query by the
fastest system's time on that query and taking the geometric mean, so **1.0
would be fastest on every query and lower is better**.

| System | Warm-run score | Warm total |
|---|---|---|
| MotherDuck Jumbo | 1.31× | 14.4 s |
| ClickHouse, local disk | 1.37× | 16.6 s |
| DuckDB, local file | 2.56× | 26.2 s |
| **Airhouse, data in S3** | **3.50×** | **34.3 s** |
| BigQuery | 6.04× | 27.3 s |
| Databricks SQL Medium | 6.37× | 32.2 s |
| Snowflake Medium (Gen2) | 6.99× | 60.3 s |

With its data in object storage, Airhouse scores ahead of BigQuery, Databricks,
and Snowflake, and behind MotherDuck and the engines that read from local disk.
A score is an average of per-query ratios, so the ratio of two scores is not a
speed-up.

<Note>
How to read these numbers:

- **Single run.** This is one run by the Airhouse team on 12 October 2026, not
  yet submitted to or reviewed by ClickBench.
- **One setting changed.** The run used a larger Parquet row-group size than
  the default. Databases provisioned today still use the smaller default until
  the new one ships.
- **Recomputed scores.** The other systems' scores are recomputed from their
  published ClickBench timings, against only the systems in this table, so
  they differ from the ClickBench website.
- **Warm runs.** The scores use warm runs, the common case for a database in
  active use. The first query after a restart reads everything from S3 and is
  Airhouse's weakest result.
- **One table, no joins.** ClickBench doesn't measure join-heavy or
  star-schema workloads.
</Note>

## Where it fits

[Airway](/guide/build/data-infrastructure/airway) pipelines land extracted data
in Airhouse, and [custom apps](/guide/build/sdk/functions) append their own
facts to it. Teams that already run a warehouse can skip Airhouse, since Oxygen
[connects to your own](/guide/build/connect-data) and the semantic model
compiles the same way wherever the data lives.
